#9939. Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription

Meanwhile, Google's homepage demo leaves a familiar button out of the picture

Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for users without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout.

Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact users with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily."

It's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and users can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability.

"With the updated search experience, users can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said.

The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back.

Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain.

In a post, Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists users' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience.  Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches."

However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present.

Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button.

Users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works."

The sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®

#9937. Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Cybercriminals using agentic pen-testing tools is a proverbial genie out of the bottle at this point, so enterprises need to get a defense plan in place right away.

A month since it went closed-source, the Artex agentic penetration testing framework is spreading faster and causing more havoc than ever. Still, cyber defenders tell Dark Reading that defending against it is largely a matter of willingness, not capability.

To recap: In August, a Chinese open source (OSS) developer released a cybercrime-grade agentic red-teaming tool called "Artex." In the months that followed, attackers and cybersecurity researchers have gradually realized just how effective Artex is at probing for vulnerabilities and turning initial access into meaningful compromise at so-called machine speed.

"Artex is what the perpetual conflict era looks like," says Yuval Itzchakov, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of A Security. "When our research team ran it against our open source benchmark, it found eight vulnerabilities in about 45 minutes, including a critical privilege escalation to admin, and chained them into a full attack path through a WAF, CAPTCHA, and MFA. All it took was a download, an install script, and a model key."

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Nothing about it is so complicated, he says, "And that's the point. Take the guardrails off an AI hacking tool, and anyone can run agentic attacks at scale. In Artex, scope is just a suggestion to the model."

Though its author de-listed the original Artex on Oct. 8, new variants continue to cause trouble. The variant du jour, "AntiFox," was recently weaponized by attackers to exploit Internet-facing Web services and their associated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. According to researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs, threat actors used their new agentic toy to breach, deploy Web shells, and execute operating system (OS) commands on compromised Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers, as well as enumerate services, expose production secrets, and manipulate Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets across AWS environments.

Notably, Arctic Wolf Labs offered relatively banal advice for organizations defending against this quite new threat: hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs), rotate and revoke relevant credentials and sessions. In fact, researchers say, there's little more to defending against Artex or AntiFox than basic cybersecurity hygiene. However, it's also important to avoid making assumptions; as GitGuardian pointed out in a blog post on AntiFox, "Blocking scanner tools won't stop these agents, and a leaked key stays dangerous until someone revokes it."

The prospect of every Tom, Dick, and Harry having an agentic attack framework in their pocket might be intimidating, but cybersecurity defenders still possess some distinct advantages.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

First off, Itzchakov points out that "Artex stops at the front door. It has no lateral movement, no Active Directory testing, and no view inside. Defenders can see their whole environment and test it continuously with the same speed and autonomy, under guardrails no one can switch off. The organizations that come out ahead will treat this as permanent and build their security around it."

In a profile of a recent incident response (IR) effort against an Artex attack, Eye Research noted another serious weakness of agentic tools in general: They're loud. "The agents left their name in pod names and probes, hammered endpoints no human would touch, and tripped detections on systems with EDR installed," it explained. "Where we had visibility, we saw them immediately."

"If you want to be positive, there are a lot of small steps you can put together in order to protect networks and organizations," says Guillaume Valadon, lead cybersecurity researcher at GitGuardian. To catch Artex or AntiFox's loudness, for example, "blue teams must have in place a security information and event management (SIEM) platform and a really good detection system, to make sure that they will detect these tools in the noise."

Related:In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More

Besides active detection, organizations would be well advised to focus on secrets management. Artex and AntiFox have proven adept at finding secrets, in part because they use ordinary commands like "git" and "grep" to find what they're looking for, instead of shipping a more easily identifiable and blockable secret scanner.

"Defenders need to be looking for exposed and dormant keys, checking Git repos for exposed secrets, and heavily implementing a defense-in-depth posture," adds Justin Moore, Arctic Wolf's director of adversary operations. "What makes these frameworks so effective is not that they’re conducting novel attacks; they’re just doing what we already know, just faster than we have seen before. Good cyber hygiene is exactly what prevents these types of attacks from being so successful, whether they’re agentic or not.”

Despite all of the positive steps organizations can take, Valadon says, "If I'm being negative, I would say that it's too late."

"For years we have been telling people that they should not output secrets — that we're finding really important hardcoded secrets everywhere, publicly. On Docker, GitHub, and so on. Now, because we have these tools that can go fast from nothing to discovery to weaponization, that makes it more difficult for blue teams," he says.

"The agentic capacity for the attacker is already here, and they're going faster and faster and faster," he notes. "So if you didn't do the right stuff before, it will be difficult for you to catch up."

The cybersecurity industry has been waiting for AI-driven cyberattacks for years now. Product marketing campaigns have hinged on agentic attacks being right around the corner. Stories of lightly AI-influenced tactics, techniques, procedures (TTPs), and malware have kept food on cyber reporters' plates. Most of the discourse has been, at best, theoretical, at worst, misleading.

A meaningful, if incomplete, turning point seems to have occurred around midyear, if not among the most sophisticated attackers, then at least in the world of middling cybercriminals.

"When we all started using ChatGPT, at that time, we were just asking it simple questions. It was fun, but it was not possible to code," Valadon explains. "And then we had agents that were more capable at coding and syncing. This year you can do it all, from end to end. You just give [an agent] a rough idea, and it will do some planning, syncing, it will build the code for you, and deploy it for you. It's getting better and better at doing the whole cycle."

He also points to Anthropic and OpenAI's warnings about OSS AI earlier this fall: "Some people are saying that we are seeing these [attack] frameworks because of Chinese open-weight models. Because if you have a big GPU, you are able to run your own offensive models with Artex."

"It's getting more and more dangerous," he says. "It's all fitting into the HuggingFace, OpenAI, Anthropic narrative [warning against attackers] having access to real offensive tools."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9935. A Deep Dive into JVM Start-up (2025)

News and views from members of the Java team at Oracle

When you start a Java application, there might be an inclination to believe that the only code being executed is the Java byte code passed to the JVM, i.e. the .class files that have been compiled by javac. The reality is that during start-up, the JVM goes through a complex series of steps to create a veritable universe for running a Java application. In this article we will walk through the steps the JVM goes through from $ java to printing Hello World. If you'd prefer video format, you can also watch this video on the Java YouTube channel:

To keep this walk-through of JVM start-up from venturing into "boil the ocean" territory, there are a few constraints I will be using to describe the process:

I will be describing the JVM start-up process as it behaves with JDK 23. You can see the JVM specification for Java SE 23 here.

I will be using the HotSpot JVM implementation as my example. This is by far the most widely used JVM implementation, with many popular JDK distributions using the HotSpot JVM or a derivative of it. Alternative JMV implementations might have a slightly different internal behaviour.

Finally the primary code example I will be using to describe the JVM start-up process will be HelloWorld, even though this is as simple an application as you can write, it will still exercise all the key areas of the JVM start-up process.

Despite these constraints, upon reading this article, you should have a reasonably comprehensive understanding of the processes the JVM goes through during start-up and why they are necessary. This knowledge could be helpful when debugging your application should issues occur during start-up, and in some niche cases improving start-up performance. Though we will cover this a bit more towards the end of the article.

When a user executes the java command, this starts the JVM start-up process by calling the JNI (Java Native Interface) function JNI_CreateJavaVM(), you can see the code for this function here. This JNI function performs several important processes itself.

The first step in the JVM start-up process is validating the user input: JVM arguments, artifact to be executed, and classpath. The below logging output shows this validation process occurring:

💡Note: You can see this logging as well by using in the JVM arg -Xlog:all=trace.

After validating the user input, the next step is to detect available system resources: processors, system memory, and system services that the JVM might use. The availability of system resources could impact decisions the JVM makes based on its internal heuristics. For example, the garbage collector the JVM selects by default will depend on the availability of CPU and system memory, however many of the JVM's internal heuristics can be overridden through the use of explicit JVM arguments.

After understanding available system resources, the JVM will begin to prepare the environment. Here the HotSpot JVM implementation generates hsprefdata (HotSpot performance data). This data is used by tools like JConsole and VisualVM to inspect and profile a JVM. This data is typically stored in a system's /tmp directory. The below is just one example of the JVM creating this profiling data, this it will continue for some time during start-up, concurrent with other processes.

An important step in the start-up of the JVM is the selection of the garbage collector (GC). Which GC is being used could have substantial impacts on the performance of an application. By default the JVM has two GCs it will choose from, Serial GC and G1 GC, unless otherwise directed.

As of JDK 23, the JVM will select the G1 GC by default, unless the system has less than 1792 MB of available system memory, and/or only a single processor, in which case Serial GC is selected. Of course other GCs might be available including: Parallel GC, ZGC, and others depending upon the specific JDK version and distribution you are using, each with their distinct performance characteristics and ideal workloads.

Around this time the JVM will look for the CDS archive. CDS, Cached Data Storage (formerly Class Data Storage), is an archive of class files that have been pre-processed, which can improve the start-up performance of the JVM. We will cover how CDS improves JVM start-up performance in during the Class Linking section. However don't commit "CDS" to memory, it's on its way out, we will cover why when we look into the future of JVM start-up later.

One of the JVM's last initialization steps is creating the method area. This is a special off-heap memory location where class data will be stored as the JVM loads it. While the method area is not located in the JVM's heap, the garbage collector still manages it. Class data stored in the method area is eligible for removal if the class loader associated with it is no longer in scope.

💡 Note: If you are using a HotSpot JVM implementation, the method area is referred to as metaspace.

Once the initial housekeeping steps have been completed, the real "meat" of the JVM start-up process begins which involves Class Loading, Linking, and Initialization.

While the JVM Specification describes these processes sequentially; sections 5.3-5.5, these processes, for a given class, won't necessarily occur in that order on a HotSpot JVM. As noted at the bottom of the chart, Resolution, part of Class Linking, could occur at any point from before Verification to after Class Initialization. Some processes, like Class Initialization, might not technically occur at all. We will cover all of this in the upcoming sections.

Class Loading is covered under section 5.3 of the JVM specification. Class Loading is a three step process of: the JVM locating the binary representation of a class or interface, deriving the class or interface from it, and loading that information into the JVM method area - which again would be referred to as "metaspace" if you are using a HotSpot JVM implementation.

One of the great powers of the JVM, and why it has become such a widely used platform, is its ability to dynamically load classes, allowing the JVM to load classes that have been generated on-demand during the JVM's runtime. This ability is used by many popular frameworks and tools, like for example Spring and Mockito. Indeed even the JVM itself performs on-demand code generation when using lambdas, as can be seen in the InnerClassLambdaMetafactory class.

The JVM allows for two ways of loading classes, either with the bootstrap class loader (5.3.1), or a custom class loader (5.3.2). The latter is a class that extends the java.lang.ClassLoader class. In practice custom class loaders would often be defined in a 3rd party library to support that library's behavior.

During this article we will only focus on the bootstrap class loader, which is a special class loader written in machine code and is provided by the JVM. It is instantiated in the latter stages of JNI_CreateJavaVM().

To better understand the process of Class Loading, we need to take a look at HelloWorld as the JVM would see it:

All classes, at some point, extend off of java.lang.Object. In order for the JVM to load HelloWorld, it first needs to load all the classes that HelloWorld explicitly and implicitly depends on. Let's take a look at all the method signatures in java.lang.Object:

The two important methods, would be public final native Class getClass() and public String toString() as both of these methods reference another class: java.lang.Class and java.lang.String respectively.

If we look at java.lang.String, it implements several interfaces:

To load java.lang.String, all its implementing interfaces must first be loaded, if we look at the logging output, we will see that these classes are loaded in the order they are defined, with java.lang.String being loaded last:

If we move over to java.lang.Class, we see it too implements several interfaces, as well as some of the same interfaces as java.lang.String: java.io.Serializable and java.lang.constant.Constable.

If we look at the JVM logs, we see that the interfaces are once again loaded in the order they are defined before java.lang.Class is loaded, except for java.io.Serializable and java.lang.constant.Constable, as they had already been loaded while loading java.lang.String.

💡 Note: Generally the JVM follows a lazy strategy for its processes, in this case Class Loading. A class is typically only loaded when it is actively referenced by another class, but as java.lang.Object is the special root class of all Java classes, the JVM will eagerly load java.lang.Class and java.lang.String. If you look at the method signatures for java.lang.Class (JavaDoc) and java.lang.String (JavaDoc) you might notice many of the classes are not loaded when executing an application like HelloWorld. For example Optional describeConstable() is never referenced, and so java.util.Optional is never loaded. This is an example of HotSpot's lazy strategy in action, or I suppose not in action.

The process of Class Loading will continue through much of the rest of JVM start-up, and in a real world application, during much of the early part of that application's lifecycle, before eventually settling down. In total the JVM will load some 450 classes in the HelloWorld scenario, and this is why I used the analogy of the JVM creating a universe when starting up, as it's doing a lot of work.

Let's continue diving into the universe of JVM start-up by looking at Class Linking.

Class Linking, covered under section 5.4 of the JVM specification, is one of the more complex processes as it includes three distinct sub-processes:

There are three other processes within Class Linking: Access Control, Method Overriding, and Method Selection, but are outside of the scope of this article.

Returning to the chart Verification, Preparation, and Resolution don't necessarily occur in the order they will be covered in this article. Resolution could happen as early as before Verification, to as late as after Class Initialization.

Verification 5.4.1, is a process of ensuring the class or interface is structurally correct. This process might kick off the loading of other classes if needed, though classes loaded as a result aren’t required to be verified or prepared themselves.

Returning to the topic of CDS, in most normal situations, JDK classes will not actively go through the Verification step. This is because one of the benefits provided by CDS is that the classes contained within the archive have already been verified, reducing the work the JVM needs to do on start-up, and as a result improving start-up performance.

If you would like to learn more about CDS, check out my Stack Walker video on the subject, our articles on dev.java on CDS, or this article inside.java article on how to include your application's classes in a CDS archive.

One class that does need to be verified would be HelloWorld, which we can see the JVM performing this in the logs:

Preparation 5.4.2 handles the initialization of static fields in a class to their default values.

To better understand this, lets use this simple example class:

Which contains three integer fields: myStaticInt, myStaticInitializedInt, and myInstanceInt.

In this example both myStaticInt and myStaticInitializedInt would be initialized to 0, the default for a primitive int type.

While myInstanceInt isn’t initialized as it’s an instance field, not a class field.

We'll cover a little later when the myStaticInt, myStaticInitializedInt fields are initialized to the values of 10 and 20.

The goal of Resolution 5.4.3 is to resolve the symbolic references in the Constant Pool of a class for use by JVM instructions.

To better understand this we will use the javap tool. This is a standard JDK command-line tool for disassembling Java .class files. Running it with the -verbose option will give a view into how the JVM interprets the classes it is loading. Let's run javap on MyClass:

The result of this command is shown below:

💡 Note: This output has been slightly truncated to remove metadata that isn't relevant to this article.

There is a lot here, so let's break it down and step through what all this means.

The below segment is MyClass's (automatically generated) default constructor, which starts with the call to the default constructor of MyClass's parent class java.lang.Object and then sets myInstanceInt to its assigned value of 30.

💡 Note: No doubt you'll have noticed the aload_0, invokespecial, bipush, putfield, and so on. These are JVM Instructions, opcode that the JVM uses to actually perform its work.

To the right of invokespecial and putfield, there are the numbers #1 and #7 respectively. These are references to MyClass's Constant Pool 4.4. Which let's take a closer at it:

Contained in the MyClass Constant Pool are all of its symbolic references. For the JVM to execute the invokespecial JVM instruction, it needs to resolve the linkage to the default constructor of java.lang.Object. Referring back to the Constant Pool, entries 1-6 provides the information needed to form this linkage.

💡 Note: is a special method javac automatically generates for each constructor in a class.

This pattern is also repeated with the putfield which references Constant Pool entry 7, which when combined with entries 8-12 provides the necessary information to resolve the linkage for setting myInstanceInt. For more on the Constant Pool check out the section in the JVM specification on it.

The reason why the Resolution process can occur from before Verification, to after Class Initialization, is that it's performed lazily, only when the JVM attempts to execute a JVM instruction in a class. Not all classes that are loaded will have a JVM instruction executed. For example the java.lang.SecurityManager class is loaded but never touched, as it's on its way out. It's also possible that there is nothing to initialize in a class, and it's automatically marked as initialized by the JVM. Which on the subject of Class Initialization...

Finally there is Class Initialization, covered under 5.5 of the JVM specification. Class Initialization, involves assigning a ConstantValue to static fields and executing any static initializers in a class if present. It is started when the JVM invokes any of new, getstatic, putstatic, or invokestatic JVM instructions on a class.

The initialization of a class is handled by the special no args method, void , which like is automatically generated by javac. The inclusion of the angle brackets (< >), is deliberate as they are not valid characters for a method name and thus prevents Java users from writing their own custom or methods.

It’s not a guarantee that a method is always created, as it’s only needed if there are static initializers or fields within a class. If a class has neither, then is not generated, and the JVM immediately marks the class as initialized if new is called on it, in effect skipping Class Initialization, and how Resolution can occur after Class Initialization.

As MyClass does have two static fields and a static initializer block, it does have a method, which back to the output of javap:

The structure of resembles , but without making a call to a parent class' constructor and JVM instructions like putstatic are used instead of putfield.

Eventually the JVM will have done enough prep work to start executing the user code inside public static void main(), where or Hello World! message is located:

In total the JVM would load some 450 classes, and some subset of that would be linked and initialized as well. On my M4 MacBook Pro, as can be seen in the logs, the entire process took just 62 milliseconds, even while performing VERY heavy logging. You can see the full log on my GitHub here.

This is actually a very exciting time for start-up on the JVM. While there have been continual refinements to the start-up process with every release of the JDK, starting with JDK 24 the first feature from Project Leyden will be merged into a mainline JDK release.

Project Leyden has the goals of reducing: start-up time, time-to-peak performance, and memory footprint, and is building upon and superseding the work done with CDS. As Project Leyden is integrated, CDS will give way to AOT, ahead-of-time. Project Leyden features will work through recording the JVMs behavior during a training run, storing that information in a cache, and then loading from that cache on subsequent start-ups. If you'd like to learn more about Project Leyden, be sure to check out this video on it.

The lead-off feature for Project Leyden will be JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking. We already covered Class Loading and Linking in this article, so the benefit of performing that work ahead of time, instead of at start-up should be quite clear now.

As covered in this article the JVM start-up process is a complex process. The ability to respond to available system resources, provide the means to inspect and profile the JVM, dynamically load classes and more, does come with a fair amount of complexity overhead.

So what can be taken from this, beyond having a deeper understanding of the JVM? There are two worth pointing out, debugging and performance, though their applicability might also be somewhat narrow.

The JVM start-up process is very reliable, and typically when errors do occur, the cause of them is often an obvious user mistake, or perhaps an issue in a 3rd party library. Hopefully a deeper understanding of what the JVM is attempting to do and why might provide some better guidance on those more persistent or difficult to understand start-up issues.

Another potential benefit is that with this knowledge you might find some small opportunities to improve the start-up performance of your application. Particularly with JEP 483 being integrated in JDK 24, moving forward Class Loading and Linking behavior could further improve start-up performance. Though I would also caution that in most use cases the 1st party code you write is often just a very small fraction of the code running on the JVM. Between the libraries, frameworks, and the JDK itself, often the code that makes up your application is just the tip of the iceberg.

#9934. An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes

No sophisticated malware or attack framework required

A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.

It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine.

“What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.”

Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one.

Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET.

OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work.

“Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.”

That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing.

The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t).

After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works.

The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems.

“It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.”

In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit.

It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then.

The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.”

While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein.

“No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.”

Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds.

“Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

#9932. Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Most organizations haven't sorted out their cryptographic estate enough to even know where they'd start with post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

The pressure is mounting for security leaders to get serious about their post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition plans, but most organizations aren't even ready to get ready for PQC.

Studies show that, yes, CISOs today do see PQC as a priority they need to plan for. However, the bulk of organizations don't have a detailed enough cryptographic inventory to help them sketch out a road map of where to start.

"When it comes to post-quantum cryptography, every company, no matter which ones you talk to, are kind of stuck in the discovery phase," says Anurag Swarnim Yadav, Ph.D., founder and CTO of startup QubitAC.

Recent numbers back his observations. According to a July study by DigiCert, while 87% of organizations say they're planning, testing, or implementing PQC, only 44% have developed transition plans or created inventories. That mirrors another study by Ponemon Institute that found only 43% of organizations have full visibility of their cryptographic estate. Those respondents reported that their inability to discover those assets and improve that visibility is their No. 1 concern about PQC migration.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Cryptography sits in Web servers, certificates, VPNs, code signing, vendor products, and all nature of assets in between. Getting every encryption use case ready for a post-quantum world will be a sweeping transition, and the latest research suggests developments in quantum computing are proceeding on a much faster timeline than originally anticipated. If an enterprise can't enumerate all the cryptography impacted, it means they're not toeing the start line for this footrace.

Getting all of those assets into post-quantum readiness will be a generational effort easily on par with the Y2K effort. Unlike Y2K, however, there's no set-in-stone deadline for post-quantum.

The closest thing is Q Day, the point when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) can break the public-key cryptography behind key exchange and digital signatures. The big problem with building a widespread sense of urgency is that nobody knows exactly when Q Day will arrive.

Estimates run from 2030 to 2040 and beyond, according to Yadav, but his own bet is that attackers could pull it off by 2029 based on how the research is shifting. The expected window until Q Day arrives keeps compressing as quantum researchers perfect their craft. Last year Google researchers calculated that breaking 2048-bit RSA encryption would take a quantum computer 20 times smaller than they had estimated in 2019. And in March Google set a 2029 target for its own PQC migration, influenced by such research and recent progress in quantum hardware.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Global governments are also starting to get firm about their own timing expectations for PQC transition in the run-up to Q Day. NIST finalized its PQC transition road map in late October, and a June executive order requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to move key establishment to post-quantum algorithms by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends that large organizations complete discovery and assessment and build an initial migration plan by 2028, then finish migrating by 2035.

Even if we don't know exactly when Q Day will come, the math behind what will happen after that day is well understood. Public-key cryptography lets two parties who have never met agree on a secret and prove who they are. It works because some math is easy to run forward and impractical to reverse. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring huge numbers, while elliptic curve cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on a related problem called the discrete logarithm.

Quantum computers use subatomic particles instead of transistors to represent data. This gives them an edge in how they process the ones and zeros of computing. For years cryptography experts have warned that a sufficiently advanced enough quantum computer could use that edge to factor huge numbers and solve discrete logarithms at a rate of efficiency unheard of from even the most advanced classical super computers.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

There's also a more immediate deadline that's brewing from what attackers are likely doing today to prepare for Q Day. It's fairly trivial for the bad guys to vacuum up high-value encrypted traffic today with the promise that they might have a chance to decrypt it at a later date. For long-lived information like financial or health details or secret sauce intellectual property, the long-game of this harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) is worth the effort for future-minded criminals.

"The data is worthless to attackers right now but becomes priceless later," Yadav explains.

He offers credit card numbers as a classic example. They stay valid for years, so a cache of encrypted numbers harvested now could still be good if Q Day lands inside that window.

In its recently finalized road map, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) pointed to HNDL as one of the main reasons the transition is so urgent. NIST mathematician and cryptographic expert Andrew Regenscheid says HNDL reframes the whole PQC timeline for critical information stores across industry and government systems.

"This information may need to remain secret for years, or even decades, into the future," he explained in a NIST Q&A this past summer. "For that kind of information, waiting until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives is waiting too long."

Considering that the most isolated cryptographic migrations can still linger for upward of a decade or longer, even a conservative 2040 estimate for Q Day should be enough to have security experts scrambling to plan PQC transitions. The scale of changes needed will take significant planning and prioritization that will need to be phased in.

"Changing these algorithms is something that's been done before. It's a complex process that takes years," Regenscheid said. "Based on our experience and the challenge of navigating the post-quantum world, we expect this process to be the most challenging one yet. The breadth of these systems and the complexity of the change will dwarf what we've done before."

The destination, at least, is defined. In 2024, NIST finalized three post-quantum standards, one for key exchange (ML-KEM) and two for digital signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), built on math that's expected to hold up against quantum computers. The harder job is finding every place RSA and elliptic curve cryptography still run, then planning how and when to swap out each use case. Because of HNDL, NIST suggests prioritizing the first transition phases around data that is particularly sensitive or has to stay secure for a long time.

In a September study on PQC readiness, Frost & Sullivan analysts emphasized how important risk-based prioritization like this will be for PQC readiness.

"A non-compliant cryptographic asset supporting a low-value application may represent limited immediate risk, while the same technology supporting sensitive information or a critical business process could require urgent remediation," they wrote.

But sorting through all the assets and ranking them depends on having a solid inventory on hand. This is why the discovery is so crucial. Frost &Sullivan concurred that the discovery process is proving to be trickier than many thought it would be.

"The inventory needs to extend beyond simply identifying algorithms to understanding the dependencies between cryptographic assets and business-critical applications," they explained.

Tools — commercial and open source — designed to assist organizations in their PQC journey are already available. These tools have their own approaches and varying levels of maturity. One tool is AC Scanner, which Yadav and QubitAC co-founder Joseph Wilson demoed at Black Hat Arsenal this past August. The free open source tool is purpose-built to kickstart the inventory process, Yadav says. It's a fast, lightweight tool that runs from command line, scans for outward facing TLS and SSH services, and creates an inventory for the IP range it's pointed at.

"You start with nothing but a domain name, and by the end you get a complete cryptographic bill of materials [CBOM]," Yadav says. The CBOM is an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols in use, and the scanner pairs it with two scores, one for overall security health and one for post-quantum readiness based on NIST's post-quantum standards.

It also doubles as an outside check on HNDL exposure. Every encrypted session starts with a key exchange, where the two sides agree on a secret. If a public-facing endpoint still uses a classical exchange, traffic an attacker records today could be unlocked later by a quantum computer. A hybrid exchange that adds post-quantum math protects that traffic, provided the client uses it, too; the scanner reports which kind each endpoint offers.

Classical endpoints are the ones most exposed to HNDL, and Yadav sees AC Scanner as giving organizations a starting point for making HNDL-aware transition plans.

Of course, any security professional will be quick to point out that a scan is just an informational snapshot. What happens after that information is in hand is what really counts. Scanning tools can kick-start discovery, but organizations need to follow up what they find with a migration plan and start executing on it. NIST'’s Regenscheid says the sooner organizations can get to these plans, the better.

"Given how long these transitions take, the organizations that start planning and begin moving to post-quantum products and services now will be in a far stronger position later," he says, adding that this is an opportunity to modernize a lot of the process. "Many steps must occur in sequence, which is why an early start is crucial."

An award-winning freelance reporter with nearly two decades of experience covering B2B cybersecurity, Ericka Chickowski has tackled every angle of security and risk for Dark Reading since 2009. Her coverage has spanned the full range of cyber topics important to every kind of cybersecurity stakeholder, including cybersecurity practitioners, CISOs, security-minded business managers, and security-aware board directors. She specializes in going deep on topics, breaking down how the technology trends affect real people, and how risk impacts the bottom line.

Some special areas of focus include: adversarial AI; AI risk and resilience; AI and agentic governance; application security (AppSec); governance, risk, and compliance (GRC); cloud security; network security; software supply chain risk; cyberinsurance; DevSecOps; enterprise risk management; and CISO career development.

In addition to Dark Reading, Ericka has written for many different IT and business publications over the years. Her byline has appeared in dozens of trade and consumer magazines, including Baseline, Consumer Digest, Channel Insider, CIO Insight, CSOOnline.com, DevOps.com, eWeek, Entrepreneur, Forbes, InformationWeek, SC Magazine, and SecurityBoulevard. She regularly contributes independent stories about AppSec and supply chain risk to the ReversingLabs Blog. She was one of the founding contributing editors for DevOps.com and has deep expertise in digital transformation and development best practices. This helps inform her stories on software risks and business resilience.

Ericka is also a prolific executive ghost writer, with experience helping cybersecurity and IT leaders bring their ideas to life. She's helped them craft important position pieces for respected publications like the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Prior to beginning her freelance career, Ericka served in a number of editorial staff roles, including West Coast Bureau Chief for SC Magazine. Before that position, she was editor-in-chief for a cluster of regional technology and lifestyle magazines in the Seattle area, as well as a beat reporter for a regional business newspaper. She holds a bachelor's degree in English from the University of Washington. Her work is well-regarded and has won multiple awards from the Society of Professional Journalists.

#9931. Arm strongarms site that hosts ad-free documentation and it may disappear

Easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!

Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

“The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

That doesn’t matter to Arm, though: As far as the lawyers are concerned, Palmisciano’s site is a copyright violation due to its use of Arm trademarks and inclusion of copyrighted reference material for the Armv9-A and Armv9-A architecture.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

“Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

"We have a responsibility to ensure Arm is the primary source of technical resources and information and to protect the Arm brand," an Arm spokesperson told us. "Striking the right balance between third parties sharing helpful peer-to-peer resources while ensuring copyrighted Arm-related technical content is accurate has been critical to building the thriving ecosystem we have today."

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

"We have recently flagged our concerns with regard to the use of Arm copyright content and the Arm brand on this website and shared the Arm trademark guidelines," Arm explained. "Our hope is to open a constructive dialogue, and we've asked that the website owner reach out as we seek to resolve this."As Palmisciano posted on HN, Arm is asking for removal of its trademark and copyrighted documentation. That, Palmisciano said, "seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful."  He also followed up around 8.30 pm GMT on Tuesday to let us know that he has not yet heard directly from Arm. ®

#9928. 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters

Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise.

In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.”

The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name.

Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests.

Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”

The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote.

Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.”

“Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.”

To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters.

That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs.

And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation.

Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility.

Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

#9923. Fund browser-grade certificate checking for every TLS client

Other software leaves users at risk while operators are responsible for timely remediation efforts across numerous platforms and application runtimes. upki brings platform-independent browser-grade protection to any TLS library, so everyone can benefit from better security and agility with minimal changes.

Help sponsor upki to make your TLS clients more secure, now and in the future.

Non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors. These trust roots are often based on browser root programs, but lack the data that allow browsers to make fine-grained trust decisions: revocation data for end entities, intermediates and roots (like CRLite and OneCRL), distrust dates and Certificate Transparency policy.

The October 2026 eMudhra incident showed the cost. Browsers blocked the affected intermediates quickly, while other clients were unable to restrict only the affected intermediates. Instead, they had to wait for platform trust store updates to remove the parent root certificates and spent significant time and effort to mitigate the impact on their applications across different platforms and environments.

upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy. Its checks only ever narrow what a client accepts: they never make it trust a certificate it would otherwise reject.

Sponsorships are annual and pay for maintainer time on the roadmap and on ongoing maintenance. We don't sell individual features; priorities are open for discussion with sponsors.

For more information, contact Dirkjan Ochtman.

Sponsors help set priorities through quarterly roadmap calls.

Clients outside the browser accept revoked end-entity certificates.

upki syncs compact CRLite filters several times a day and checks revocation offline.

When root programs distrust a CA or intermediate, other clients keep trusting it until a trust store package update arrives, as the eMudhra incident showed.

upki will ship OneCRL data, so distrust takes effect at the next cache update.

Post-quantum signatures would add kilobytes to every TLS handshake. Merkle Tree Certificates can bring down the costs, but clients need landmarks delivered ahead of time to minimize handshake overhead.

upki will distribute landmarks alongside its other data.

Clients that don't enforce Certificate Transparency accept certificates that were never publicly logged, so misissuance can go unnoticed. Clients also don't benefit from certificate transparency logs blocking compromised/distrusted roots from obtaining proof of inclusion.

upki will deliver and maintain an up-to-date log list and policy inputs, so applications don't have to configure logs manually.

Servers that send an incomplete certificate chain work in browsers but fail verification in other clients.

upki will ship the known intermediate certificates, so clients can complete the chain as browsers do, without expensive network fetching.

Root changes, including private PKI roots, reach machines through OS packages or configuration management, which can be slow and uneven across a fleet.

upki's sync mechanism could distribute root sets to every machine.

The checks only protect applications whose TLS stack uses upki.

upki could gain native support in OpenSSL upstream, GnuTLS, NSS or in language runtimes.

Every check depends on data that's refreshed several times a day, on upstream sources and formats that keep changing, and on prompt fixes when security issues come up.

Sponsorship pays for releases, security response, dependency updates, keeping the data pipeline running and in step with upstream changes, supporting distribution packagers and maintaining C2SP specifications.

upki lives in the rustls organization on GitHub and is dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and MIT.

#9919. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:

That one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

Add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.
